plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 35: Geometric Optics and Image Formation
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single ray diagram of image formation by a converging lens. A biconvex lens, shaded pale blue with a vertical dashed line through its center, stands upright on a horizontal optical axis. A red upward arrow to the left of the lens is the object, and its height is marked h_o by a double-headed arrow at the far left edge. Two red dots on the axis mark the focal points, each labeled F, one on either side of the lens, and a bracket from the lens center to the right-hand focal point is labeled f. Three rays leave the tip of the object. Ray 1, in red, travels parallel to the axis and bends at the lens to pass through the far focal point. Ray 2, in green, runs straight through the center without deviation. Ray 3, in purple, passes through the near focal point before emerging parallel to the axis. The three rays cross below the axis on the right, where a short red downward arrow of height h_i marks the inverted image. Horizontal brackets beneath the axis give the object distance d_o and the image distance d_i. Because each ray follows a different simple rule, their common crossing point fixes the position and size of the image by drawing alone, and the image produced here is one that could be caught on a screen.

interactionPlan.concept: Three easy-to-draw principal rays from a point on the object all converge at one point after a converging lens, and that crossing point locates and sizes the real, inverted image described by 1/d_o + 1/d_i = 1/f.
elements: Horizontal black optical axis spanning the full canvas width, with the plotted world domain tightened to roughly x = -4 to +5 focal lengths and y = -3 to +3 so object, lens, rays and image fill the frame at textbook scale
Fat biconvex lens centered on the axis: pale blue fill, darker blue outline, drawn with a large bulge control offset so the two convex faces visibly swell (thick lens body, not a sliver)
Short vertical black dashed principal-plane line through the lens center, trimmed to roughly the lens height (does not run the full height of the canvas)
Red upward object arrow standing on the axis left of the lens, thick shaft and solid arrowhead
Vertical double-headed black dimension arrow beside the object labeled h_o (subscript rendered inline, never wrapping)
Red dot on the axis one focal length left of the lens, labeled F in large bold black type below the axis
Red dot on the axis one focal length right of the lens, labeled F in large bold black type below the axis
Horizontal double-headed bracket from lens center to the right focal point labeled f
Ray 1 (red): from the object tip parallel to the axis, refracting at the principal plane and passing through the far focal point, continuing down-right past the image
Ray 2 (green): from the object tip straight through the lens center undeviated, continuing down-right
Ray 3 (purple): from the object tip through the near focal point, refracting at the lens and emerging parallel to the axis below it

Large bold colored ray numerals: '1' placed above the horizontal incoming segment of ray 1 (well clear of the object arrow), '2' offset along the slanted path of ray 2 between object and lens, '3' offset along the slanted path of ray 3 between object and near focal point
Mid-ray arrowheads on each colored ray showing propagation direction
Short thick red downward image arrow below the axis at the three-ray crossing point (real, inverted image)
Vertical double-headed black dimension arrow beside the image labeled h_i
Horizontal double-headed bracket below the axis from object foot to lens labeled d_o
Horizontal double-headed bracket below the axis from lens to image foot labeled d_i
Compact readout panel showing d_o, d_i, f, magnification m = -d_i/d_o and image type (real/inverted or virtual/upright), with subscripts typeset inline so labels stay on one line
Dashed backward extensions of the refracted rays plus an upright red virtual-image arrow on the object side, shown only when the object sits inside the focal point

interactions.teaches: Moving the object changes where the rays cross: as d_o decreases toward f the image races away from the lens and grows, and inside f the rays diverge into an upright virtual image — the lens equation made visible.
interactions.label: Object distance d_o (units of f)

interactions.teaches: Each principal ray obeys one simple rule (parallel-in → through F, straight through the center, through F → parallel-out), yet all three land on the same image point, so any two suffice to construct the image.

The measured drawing IS the algebra: hiding the f, d_o, d_i, h_o and h_i markings leaves the bare ray construction, showing that the geometry alone already determines every quantity in the lens and magnification equations.
interactions.label: Dimension annotations

demo_steps.title: The measured figure
demo_steps.narration: The full textbook figure appears as in the source: object arrow of height h_o, fat biconvex lens with its dashed principal plane, focal points F on each side, and brackets for f, d_o and d_i already drawn along with the inverted image of height h_i.

demo_steps.title: Three rays, three rules
demo_steps.narration: Rays 1, 2 and 3 all leave the same point at the object's tip. Click any one to isolate it: parallel-then-through-F, straight-through-the-center, or through-F-then-parallel.

demo_steps.title: Strip the annotations
demo_steps.narration: Hide the brackets and height arrows and only the rays remain — yet they still cross at exactly the same point. The image location is a consequence of the geometry, not of the labels.

demo_steps.title: Bring the measurements back
demo_steps.narration: Restore the overlay and read the numbers: h_i/h_o equals -d_i/d_o, and the three distances satisfy 1/d_o + 1/d_i = 1/f.

demo_steps.title: Push the object far away
demo_steps.narration: With the object far from the lens the rays converge just beyond the far focal point: d_i shrinks toward f and the inverted image becomes small.

demo_steps.title: Slide it toward the focal point
demo_steps.narration: As d_o approaches f the refracted rays become nearly parallel, d_i shoots off to the right and the inverted image grows enormous.

demo_steps.title: Inside the focal point
demo_steps.narration: Closer than f, the refracted rays diverge; dashed backward extensions meet at an upright, magnified virtual image on the object side — the magnifying-glass case, with d_i now negative.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Three rays drawn by three different simple rules meet at one point — that single intersection is the image, giving its position, size and orientation without any algebra.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Wide landscape layout with a tight world window (about x = -4 to +5 and y = -3 to +3 in focal-length units) so the object, lens, ray fan and image fill the canvas at the same scale as the source. A thin black optical axis runs across the middle. A FAT pale-blue biconvex lens with a darker blue outline sits at the origin — use a generous bezier bulge so the lens body is clearly thick — and a short black dashed vertical line through its center spans only about the lens height. The object is a thick red upward arrow on the axis to the left; a thin black double-headed arrow beside it is labeled h_o. Small red dots sit one focal length left and right of the lens, each labeled F in large bold black type below the axis, and a black double-headed bracket from lens center to the right F is labeled f. Three rays leave the object tip: ray 1 red, horizontal to the lens then sloping down through the right focal point; ray 2 green, straight through the lens center; ray 3 purple, sloping down through the left focal point then horizontal to the right. Their bold numerals use a large font: '1' sits above its horizontal segment near the middle of that run, '2' and '3' sit offset perpendicular to their slanted segments partway between object and lens — none of them crowd the object arrow. Mid-ray arrowheads show direction. The refracted rays cross below the axis right of the lens where a short thick red downward arrow marks the real inverted image, with a labeled h_i dimension arrow beside it. Below the axis, black double-headed brackets span object-to-lens (d_o) and lens-to-image (d_i). Dimension annotations render by DEFAULT; the toggle only hides them, leaving the bare ray construction. All dimension and F labels use an enlarged base font size, and every subscript is typeset inline (single-line labels in both the figure and the control panel). Clicking a ray thickens it to full opacity while the other two fade to light gray and rings the relevant marker (near F, lens center, or far F). In the virtual-image regime the diverging rays gain dashed backward extensions to an upright red image arrow on the object side and the d_i bracket flips to the left and is annotated as negative.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for object distance d_o: learner drags the object toward or away from the converging lens; the three principal rays redraw and the image distance d_i and height h_i update, including inversion when a real image forms; the lens equation tradeoff between object distance and image position becomes visible.
- Click on ray 1, ray 2, or ray 3: learner selects a principal ray rule; the chosen ray is highlighted through the lens while the matching focal or center path marker is emphasized; the learner sees why three different easy-to-draw rays agree on the same image point.

authoredContext:
Consider an object some distance away from a converging lens, as shown in the figure. To find the location and size of the image, we trace the paths of selected light rays originating from one point on the object, in this case, the tip of the arrow. The figure shows three rays from many rays that emanate from the tip of the arrow. These three rays can be traced by using the ray-tracing rules given above.

Several important distances appear in the figure. As for a mirror, we define do to be the object distance, or the distance of an object from the center of a lens. The image distance di is defined to be the distance of the image from the center of a lens. The height of the object and the height of the image are indicated by ho and hi, respectively. Images that appear upright relative to the object have positive heights, and those that are inverted have negative heights. By using the rules of ray tracing and making a scale drawing with paper and pencil, like that in the figure, we can accurately describe the location and size of an image. But the real benefit of ray tracing is in visualizing how images are formed in a variety of situations.

Although three rays are traced in this figure, only two are necessary to locate a point of the image. It is best to trace rays for which there are simple ray-tracing rules.

Ray tracing is used to locate the image formed by a lens. Rays originating from the same point on the object are traced—the three chosen rays each follow one of the rules for ray tracing, so that their paths are easy to determine. The image is located at the point where the rays cross. In this case, a real image—one that can be projected on a screen—is formed.

Figure shows the cross section of a bi-convex lens. Three rays originate from the top of an object and enter the lens. Ray 1 is parallel to the optical axis. Ray 2 crosses the center of the lens. Ray 3 crosses the focal point in front of the lens. All rays converge on the other side at the top of an inverted image. Ray 1 crosses the focal point behind the lens. Ray 2 is undeviated. Ray 3 becomes parallel to the optical axis. The object distance and image distances are d subscript o and d subscript I respectively. The object and image heights are h subscript o and h subscript I respectively. The focal length is f.

elements: Horizontal optical axis spanning the full width of the figure
Biconvex lens at center, pale blue fill with darker blue outline, tall and narrow
Vertical black dashed line through the lens center (principal plane / center line)
Red upward arrow to the left of the lens representing the object, standing on the axis
Double-headed vertical arrow at far left labeled h_o measuring object height
Red dot on the axis to the left of the lens labeled F (near focal point)
Red dot on the axis to the right of the lens labeled F (far focal point)
Horizontal double-headed bracket from lens center to right focal point labeled f

Ray 2 (green): from object tip straight through lens center undeviated, continues down-right
Ray 3 (purple): from object tip through the near focal point, refracts at lens, emerges parallel to the axis to the right
Small numeric ray labels '1' (red), '2' (green), '3' (purple) placed near each incoming ray with arrowheads showing direction of travel
Short red downward arrow below the axis on the right at the ray crossing point = inverted real image
Double-headed vertical arrow labeled h_i measuring image height below the axis
Horizontal double-headed bracket below the axis from object to lens labeled d_o
Horizontal double-headed bracket below the axis from lens to image labeled d_i
Arrowheads mid-ray indicating propagation direction on each colored ray
Optional readout panel showing d_o, d_i, f, magnification m = -d_i/d_o, and image type (real/inverted vs virtual/upright)

interactions.teaches: Moving the object changes where the rays cross: as d_o decreases toward f the image races away from the lens and grows, and inside f the rays diverge and the image becomes virtual and upright — the lens equation 1/d_o + 1/d_i = 1/f made visible.
interactions.label: Object distance d_o (in units of f)

interactions.teaches: Each principal ray obeys one simple rule (parallel-in → through F, straight through the center, through F → parallel-out), yet all three land on the same image point — so any two of them are enough to construct the image.
The geometric drawing and the algebraic quantities are the same thing: the brackets for f, d_o, d_i and the arrows for h_o, h_i are exactly the terms in the lens and magnification equations.

demo_steps.title: The setup
demo_steps.narration: A red arrow object stands on the optical axis to the left of a converging lens, with focal points F marked one focal length f on each side. Nothing has been drawn yet except the object and the lens.

demo_steps.title: Three rays, three rules
demo_steps.narration: Rays 1, 2 and 3 leave the same point at the object's tip. Click any one of them to isolate it and see its rule highlighted: parallel-then-through-F, straight-through-center, or through-F-then-parallel.

demo_steps.title: They agree on one point
demo_steps.narration: All three refracted rays cross below the axis at a single point. A short downward red arrow there is the real, inverted image — light actually passes through it, so it could be caught on a screen.

demo_steps.title: Measuring the drawing
demo_steps.narration: Switch on the measurement overlay: brackets appear for d_o, d_i and f, and arrows for h_o and h_i. The ratio h_i/h_o equals -d_i/d_o, and the three distances satisfy 1/d_o + 1/d_i = 1/f.

demo_steps.title: Push the object far away
demo_steps.narration: With the object far from the lens, the rays converge just beyond the far focal point: d_i shrinks toward f and the image becomes small and strongly reduced.

demo_steps.title: Slide it toward the focal point
demo_steps.narration: As d_o approaches f, the refracted rays become nearly parallel, d_i shoots off to the right and the inverted image grows enormous — the tradeoff between object and image distance in action.

demo_steps.title: Inside the focal point
demo_steps.narration: Move the object closer than f and the refracted rays diverge; extending them backward gives an upright, magnified virtual image on the object side — the magnifying-glass case.

plan.keyInsight: Three rays drawn by three different simple rules meet at the same point — that single intersection is the image, so ray tracing alone gives you both where the image is and how big and which way up it is.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Wide landscape layout. A thin black horizontal optical axis runs across the middle. A tall pale-blue biconvex lens with a darker blue outline sits slightly right of center, with a black vertical dashed line through its axis of symmetry. The object is a thick red upward arrow standing on the axis well to the left; a thin black double-headed arrow at the far left margin labels its height h_o. Two small red dots sit on the axis, one a focal length left of the lens and one a focal length right, each labeled F in black below the axis; a black horizontal bracket with arrowheads from the lens center to the right-hand F is labeled f. Three rays emanate from the object tip: ray 1 red, horizontal until the lens then sloping down through the right focal point and continuing off the lower right; ray 2 green, a straight line from tip through the lens center continuing down-right; ray 3 purple, sloping down through the left focal point, reaching the lens and then running horizontally to the right below the axis. Small bold colored numerals 1, 2, 3 sit just above their respective incoming rays with mid-ray arrowheads. The three refracted rays intersect below the axis right of the lens where a short thick red downward arrow marks the inverted image, with a thin black double-headed arrow beside it labeled h_i. Below the axis, black double-headed brackets span object-to-lens (d_o) and lens-to-image (d_i). When the overlay toggle is off, only the rays, lens, object, image and F dots are visible; when on, all brackets, height arrows and a small numeric readout of d_o, d_i, f and m appear. Highlighted rays on click render at full opacity and thicker stroke while the other two dim to light gray, and the relevant marker (near F, lens center dot, or far F) is emphasized with a ring. In the virtual-image regime the diverging refracted rays get dashed backward extensions to an upright red image arrow on the object side, and the d_i bracket is drawn on the left and annotated as negative.

discrepancies: Default (step-0) view omits every dimension annotation that the source shows as part of the static figure — the f, d_o and d_i brackets along the bottom and the h_o / h_i height arrows with tick marks; these are hidden behind the 'Measurement overlay' checkbox instead of being on by default.

Composition is zoomed far out: the x-domain runs −6.6…9.4 while all content lives between −2.5 and ~2, so the diagram occupies only the left ~40% of the canvas with a long empty axis stretching right, making everything (arrows, F dots, ray numbers) much smaller than in the source, which fills its frame.

The biconvex lens is drawn much thinner (nearly a sliver) than the visibly fat, shaded lens of the source, and the dashed principal-plane line extends past the lens top/bottom in a way the source's dashed line does not.

Ray-number labels 1, 2 and 3 sit crowded next to the object arrow (the '3' abuts the object/ray 1 region) rather than being spread along their respective rays as in the source, and they are noticeably smaller than the source's bold numerals.
The UI panel text wraps badly — 'Object distance d o = 2.50 f' and the overlay checkbox label break subscripts onto separate lines, producing five lines of fragmented text.

The image arrow lacks the source's clear h_i measurement arrow/tick pair beside it in the default state; only a plain arrow plus a small grey circle (an added element not in the source) marks the convergence point.

Their bold numerals use a large font: '1' sits above its horizontal segment near the middle of that run, '2' and '3' sit offset perpendicular to their slanted segments partway between object and lens — none of them crowd the object arrow. Mid-ray arrowheads show direction. The refracted rays cross below the axis right of the lens where a short thick red downward arrow marks the real inverted image, with a labeled h_i dimension arrow beside it. Below the axis, black double-headed brackets span object-to-lens (d_o) and lens-to-image (d_i). Dimension annotations render by DEFAULT; the toggle only hides them, leaving the bare ray construction. All dimension and F labels use an enlarged base font size, and every subscript is typeset inline (single-line labels in both the figure and the control panel). Clicking a ray thickens it to full opacity while the other two fade to light gray and rings the relevant marker (near F, lens center, or far F). In the virtual-image regime the diverging rays gain dashed backward extensions to an upright red image arrow on the object side and the d_i bracket flips to the left and is annotated as negative.

interactions.teaches: Moving the object changes where the rays cross: as d_o decreases toward f the image races away from the lens and grows, and inside f the rays diverge into an upright virtual image — the lens equation made visible.
interactions.label: Object distance d_o (units of f)

interactions.teaches: Each principal ray obeys one simple rule (parallel-in → through F, straight through the center, through F → parallel-out), yet all three land on the same image point, so any two suffice to construct the image.

The measured drawing IS the algebra: hiding the f, d_o, d_i, h_o and h_i markings leaves the bare ray construction, showing that the geometry alone already determines every quantity in the lens and magnification equations.

demo_steps.title: The measured figure
demo_steps.narration: The full textbook figure appears as in the source: object arrow of height h_o, fat biconvex lens with its dashed principal plane, focal points F on each side, and brackets for f, d_o and d_i already drawn along with the inverted image of height h_i.

demo_steps.title: Three rays, three rules
demo_steps.narration: Rays 1, 2 and 3 all leave the same point at the object's tip. Click any one to isolate it: parallel-then-through-F, straight-through-the-center, or through-F-then-parallel.

demo_steps.title: Strip the annotations
demo_steps.narration: Hide the brackets and height arrows and only the rays remain — yet they still cross at exactly the same point. The image location is a consequence of the geometry, not of the labels.

demo_steps.title: Bring the measurements back
demo_steps.narration: Restore the overlay and read the numbers: h_i/h_o equals -d_i/d_o, and the three distances satisfy 1/d_o + 1/d_i = 1/f.

demo_steps.title: Push the object far away
demo_steps.narration: With the object far from the lens the rays converge just beyond the far focal point: d_i shrinks toward f and the inverted image becomes small.

demo_steps.title: Slide it toward the focal point
demo_steps.narration: As d_o approaches f the refracted rays become nearly parallel, d_i shoots off to the right and the inverted image grows enormous.

demo_steps.title: Inside the focal point
demo_steps.narration: Closer than f, the refracted rays diverge; dashed backward extensions meet at an upright, magnified virtual image on the object side — the magnifying-glass case, with d_i now negative.
